Many of the learned, indeed, reject that word, and maintain that it is used improperly when a wife is said to have a husband, or a husband a wife, or a father a son, or a son his parent; because they assert that what has the one having [it] cannot be had: but they think it more correctly said that a husband belongs to a wife, or a wife to a husband, a father to a son, a master to servants. For they contend that the force of this word lies in this, that it cannot signify both having someone and being had.
CHAPTER XVII. — On the post-predicaments.

At length, having crossed as it were the straits of a great sea, we have finished the number of the categories, not unpersuasively, I think, for the learned, and clearly enough for those who wish to learn: but certain things remain which forbid us to touch the end of this book. For in the individual categories contrariety was treated, when we said which admitted a contrary and which rejected it. Yet no treatment has so far shown what the contrary itself is: and certain words still remain whose force and proper sense ought to be explained. For which reason let us pass to the necessary treatment of opposites.
CHAPTER XVIII. — On opposites. Three species of contraries.

There are four species of opposites: for one thing is opposed to another, first, either in the form of the category which is called relation; second, or in the manner of contraries; third, or of those concerning which a having or a privation is said to be about us (here indeed we should take 'having' from the verb 'to have', not, as we defined above, that a state is a certain lasting disposition of the mind); in the fourth way, when we either affirm or deny something: for example, let us set out an example from those that are called relatives. The first [kind of] opposite appears [as] the double to the single, or a father to a son. Let the second, the example of contraries, be bad to good. The third, of those that are spoken of by having and privation, as blindness and sight. The fourth, of those in which there is negation and affirmation, as 'he runs', 'he does not run'. The distinction between contraries and relatives is evident to those who consider [it]: for things called relatives are named from what is opposed to them; for the single is the opposite of the double, and the double the opposite of the single: but contraries have what they are called from themselves, and do not need another. For who would say 'the bad of the good', or who 'the good of the bad'? This, then, is the lucid and clear distinction between these two species which come from opposites. Contraries themselves are divided into three species: for either they have a mean, that is, they have something between them; or they are without a mean; or, as reason has found in certain cases, they have a mean indeed, but its name does not appear, unless it is made up from the negation of each opposite. Those with a mean, then, are these, white and black, between which, since pale or dusky can arise, these opposites are called mediated. In those that are mediated, it is not necessary that one of the two opposites be found in a body: for if it is not black, it can be dusky; or if white is lacking, pale can be found. But of those opposites which are not mediated, one of the two must necessarily occur, as is health and sickness. Of these there is no mean, because human bodies must necessarily hold either health or sickness. But those which have a mean indeed, though it lacks a name unless it is formed from the negation of the opposites, are these, just and unjust: there is something in the middle, but it has no name; and so the negation of each opposite creates a name for it, so that we call that which is in the middle neither just nor unjust. Now let us go over more carefully those opposites which arise through having and privation: for in these it must be observed that both are in the same matter, in the same place, at the proper time. Blindness and sight are in the same matter; for they consist in seeing and not seeing. They are also in the same place; for both blindness and sight have their place in the eyes. Most of all, however, the fitness of the time is required in these: for no one is rightly called bald unless at the time when he ought to have hair he does not have it: nor can anyone call toothless, whom the Greeks call *nōdos*, an infant to whom tender age has so far denied teeth. For privation, which in Greek is called *sterēsis*, has this force, that it shows that someone had something by nature and does not have it. Among these things we should remember that it is one thing to be sight and blindness, another to have sight and to be deprived of it; lest, if we judge these to be the same, the reasoning should seem confused. But if anyone thinks this doubtful or too little certain, let him notice what follows each thing. For if the blind and blindness were the same, both would be said of one [thing]: but we say a man is blind; yet a man cannot be called blindness: it is clear, therefore, that it is one thing to be blind, another to be blindness. Nor are affirmation and negation the same as the things that fall under affirmation and negation. For an affirmation or negation is a word affirming or denying something; but the things found under them are different, as is 'Socrates is discoursing', 'Socrates is not discoursing'. Yet all are likewise held to be opposed to one another. Sometimes, however, evils are opposed to evils, whenever the means between contraries are good, as is deficiency and excess, which the Greeks call *endeia kai hyperbolē*. For between these two evils opposed to each other, moderation is sought as the mean. Following this reasoning the Peripatetics said that the virtues are means, so that they called more than is just *pleonexia*, less than is just *meionexia*: between which evils they placed justice in the middle. Similarly, between cunning and dullness they placed prudence; between lust and insensibility, which the Greeks call *anaisthēsia*, temperance is set; between timidity and rashness, courage. Thus reason, searching thoroughly, has found a certain hidden kind of opposites, so that sometimes evils are found to be contrary to evils. But Aristotle explained more fully and in many ways the properties and differences of these four species which come from opposites: for us, however, let it suffice to have set out both genus and species, lest, occupied with minuter matters, we wear down the necessary ones with tedium.
CHAPTER XIX. — On the prior.

One thing is said to be prior to another in five ways: the first of these is when we say that someone is older in time. The second way is that in which something arises from a prior thing, but when the prior perishes the second perishes, while when the second perishes the prior remains unharmed. So one is naturally prior to two: for two arises from it, but two cannot exist without one, while without two the standing of one remains. And when two exists, one must exist, but when one appears, no necessity compels two to exist. In the third way a certain order makes one thing prior to another, as we find in the disciplines and the liberal arts: for in grammar the prior thing is to learn the forms and names of the individual letters, then to come to know the joinings of syllables, then to take in the notion of words: last of all we must take up the use of speech, for the sake of which we come to know all its parts, as members running before it. And in rhetoric the place of the prior is similarly set: for first we deliver the proem, then the narration, after that the refutation, then the confirmation; last the epilogue is placed. With these examples, then, let it suffice to have shown the third mode of the prior. The fourth mode is not very plausible, and is set out by Aristotle himself as something he disapproves of: as when the common people are accustomed to call those better or more distinguished in fortune 'prior'. But in my opinion the force of this [sense of] prior has been rejected. These are the four modes of what is called prior: but a certain more hidden fifth is added, whenever, of two things which convert with each other, that one is rather [prior] which makes the other be: so, for example, if there is a man, we rightly call him a rational, mortal animal capable of laughter. And if this definition of man is true, it is true that there is a man. So each converts with the other, that is, both that the definition of man is true, and that the man of the definition is true. But since the definition could not be true unless the nature of man first appeared, therefore of these two, which we said convert with each other, man holds the place of the prior, whose existence expresses the truth of his definition.
CHAPTER XX. — On 'simultaneous'.

It follows that we should express the proper sense of the word by which we say that certain things are simultaneous. For reason seems to require that after the treatment of the prior we should discuss those things which are affirmed to be simultaneous. Things are called simultaneous, then, in three ways: when any things exist or appear together at one time, so that neither of the two is prior or follows the other, but the rising of both seems to be common, as heat and brightness in the sun. The second place belongs to those which are naturally simultaneous, yet neither of them provides for the other: for example, if we set down the single and the double, they must be naturally simultaneous, but neither does the double make the single be, nor does the single produce the double. At this point we ought not to be confused, lest, since when we were treating things said in relation we said that to be a relative is what depends on another, we seem now to be treating [the matter] against what was defined above. For we argued that all things said in relation are said from another, not that they are from another: nor is there any error, if one examines more carefully the weight of our words. The third place is whenever things flowing from the same genus seem to be simultaneous by nature, but are distinguished by species: nor do they provide anything for each other in what they are said to be, as is animal; the genus is the same, but the species are widely distinct. Nor does anything winged grant to the footed that it should be, nor the footed to the winged, nor in general does one supply any substance to the other in what it is; and none is prior to another, but all arise together, sprung from animal, that is, from one genus.
CHAPTER XXI. — On motion.

Every change, which in Greek is *metabolē*, comes about in three ways: either from non-subject into subject, as is rising or birth, which the Greeks call *genesis*; or from subject into non-subject, as is perishing or corruption, which the Greeks called *phthora*; or from subject into subject, as is motion, which in Greek is called *kinēsis*. But motion itself also has three species, that is, increase, diminution, alteration of quality or of place. These were called by the Greeks *auxēsis*, *meiōsis*, *alloiōsis*, or *phora*. For they wished alteration with respect to place to be called *phora*, which we too have preferred to call 'transition', following the teachers. But this order, which we have at present set out with careful examination, as though differing from that book which is called the Categories, Aristotle himself also expounded in the books on nature; in the Categories, however, following brevity in teaching, he did not hesitate to take the species for the genus, that is, motion for change: so that he said six species were subordinate to motion as though to a genus: *genesis*, *phthora*, *auxēsis*, *meiōsis*, *alloiōsis poiotētos*, *tēn kata topon metabolēn*. These we have called in Latin rising, perishing, increase, diminution, alteration of quality, transition of place. These six species are distinguished from one another by every account: unless perhaps to someone understanding too little learnedly, alteration of quality, that is *alloiōsis*, should seem to occur also when the others exist, so that when something is born, or perishes, or grows, or is diminished, alteration too should then be said to have taken place. But reason teaches that this is false: for things which grow or are diminished are changed in quantity, not altered in quality. For alteration properly belongs to quality. We must remember, however, that change is one thing and alteration another. For change is the genus, alteration a species subordinate to motion, which we have called a species of change. Finally, so that the distinction between them may be clear, let us set down a geometrical example. If you divide a larger square, which is drawn, by lines running through the middle into small squares, and afterwards take one small square away from it, you have diminished the larger square: but if in the place of what was taken away you add a gnomon, which is set in the shape of a half-circle, you have given back to the larger square more than you had taken away: and this belongs to quantity, not to quality, and is attributed to change rather than to alteration, and so they differ very greatly from each other. Now difference in all things comes about in three ways: either in matter, or in workmanship, or in both. In matter, if there are two similar rings, and one is gold, the other silver; in workmanship, if dissimilar rings are made from gold; in both, if a ring is gold and a stylus silver. It is clear, then, that these species of change are joined to one another neither in matter, nor in workmanship, nor in both: indeed, they are so separated that some of them even seem contrary to one another. For who would doubt that *phthora* is contrary to *genesis*, that is, perishing to rising, and diminution to increase? Alteration too, whether of quality or of place, though not of the same number of species, nevertheless has something which seems contrary to it. For alteration of quality is when something becomes black from white or white from black, which are manifestly contrary to each other. Alteration of place too, which we have called transition, admits the contrariety of upper and lower, and therefore it is evident that it too has contraries.
CHAPTER XXII. — Conclusion of the work.

These are the things, dearest son, which, having attained them by continual labour, since the teaching of Themistius, the outstanding philosopher of our time, was not lacking to us, we have turned from Greek into Latin for your benefit; that is, so that from these too you may receive the good fruit of the study that proceeded from us, if desire for other things, which are slippery and empty, has held you back [as] not unlike us. For we have omitted nothing in this book which could either delight those already learned, or instruct the unlearned more clearly.
